content: The American College of Chest Physicians (ACCP) is a professional medical organization composed of physicians and non-physician specialists who focus on chest medicine. This field encompasses pulmonology, thoracic surgery, and critical care medicine. The title Fellow of the College of Chest Physicians (FCCP) is awarded to physicians who specialize in pulmonology, thoracic surgery, or critical care medicine. This designation is used as a post-nominal title, such as John Citizen, MD, FCCP. To qualify for this fellowship, a physician in the United States or Canada must be board-certified in both a primary specialty and an applicable subspecialty, have at least 18 months of experience in the field, and be sponsored by two current FCCP fellows. Doctorally-prepared nurses are also eligible for this fellowship. Physicians outside the United States and Canada are eligible as well, provided they have at least three years of experience in their field after completing their training. International fellows are also granted the FCCP designation. The ACCP publishes a medical journal called Chest, which serves as a resource for research and advancements in chest medicine. The ACCP provides classifications for recommendations regarding diagnostic and therapeutic procedures: Class I: There is evidence and/or general agreement that a specific diagnostic procedure or treatment is beneficial, useful, and effective. Class II: There is conflicting evidence and/or a divergence of opinion regarding the usefulness or efficacy of a treatment or procedure. Class IIa: The weight of evidence or opinion leans in favor of the treatment or procedure being useful or effective. Class IIb: The usefulness or efficacy of the treatment or procedure is less well established by evidence or opinion. Class III: There is evidence or general agreement that the treatment or procedure is not useful or effective and, in some cases, may be harmful. The ACCP also categorizes the level of evidence supporting these recommendations: Level A: Data are derived from multiple randomized clinical trials or meta-analyses. Level B: Data are derived from a single randomized clinical trial or large non-randomized studies. Level C: Recommendations are based on expert consensus, small studies, retrospective studies, or registries.
